newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Holbrooke holds marathon talks on Bosnia mission.
newsitem.headline: Holbrooke holds marathon talks on Bosnia mission.

text.p: U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke met leaders of Bosnia's rival factions into the small hours of Friday morning, pressing for full compliance with the peace treaty he brokered 18 months ago.

He plans to meet next with Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic on Friday morning, encouraging her in her power struggle with former leader and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic, then head to Belgrade for talks with the Bosnian Serbs' main patron, Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic.
The Serb, Moslem and Croat members of Bosnia's collective presidency resumed talks under Holbrooke's mediation at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT).

The American told reporters that it was too early to say whether the leaders would reach agreement on a number of disputes, including the distribution of ambassadorial posts and the design of a joint currency.
"We are in the middle of discussions...So I am not going to say whether we're going to get anything or not," he said.

Holbrooke, architect of the treaty that halted four years of war, returned to the Balkans this week to lean on political leaders in Bosnia, Croatia and Yugoslavia in a bid to speed up the stalled peace process.

Accompanied by U.S. envoy to Bosnia, Robert Gelbard, he held several hours of talks on Thursday with the multi-ethnic central cabinet and members of Bosnia's collective presidency, including Serb hardliner Momcilo Krajisnik.
An aide to the Moslem chairman of the presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, said no progress was made in talks on the design of a new currency.

Whatever the outcome of the presidency session, diplomats said the main aim of Holbrooke's visit was to make clear that Washington would not tolerate Bosnian Serb hardliners trying to undermine the peace accords.

Diplomats says that when they get to Belgrade Holbrooke and Gelbard would threaten Milosevic with economic sanctions unless he abides by his Dayton commitments, which include handing over indicted war criminals such as Karadzic.
Gelbard said that Yugoslavia risked further economic isolation if it failed to abide by the peace treaty.

"The point is the international community is very frustrated and there could well be additional adverse consequences if the right decisions are not taken by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia," he said.
It was Holbrooke's first visit to the region since he negotiated a deal last year that forced Karadzic to step down as Bosnian Serb president.

Under the agreement which was signed by Milosevic, Karadzic was supposed to stay out of politics. One year later, Karadzic and his allies persist in attempting to circumvent the Dayton accords which divided Bosnia into autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat territories ruled by a small central government.
